---
title: "Simulated Treatment Comparison"
---

## Introduction {#sec-stc-intro}

The previous chapter repaired a failing indirect comparison by reweighting. Matching-adjusted indirect
comparison (MAIC) leaves the outcomes untouched and bends the *sample* until its covariate moments match
the target, so that a weighted average of the observed outcomes estimates what the trial would have found
in the target population. This chapter develops the other half of the population-adjustment dichotomy. The
**simulated treatment comparison** (STC) of @caro2010stc leaves the *sample* untouched and bends a *model*:
it fits an outcome regression to the individual patient data (IPD), then uses the fitted regression
surface to predict what the outcomes would have been in the target population. Where MAIC is the indirect
comparison analogue of inverse-probability weighting, STC is the analogue of outcome regression, or
g-computation, of Chapter 10 (@thm-g-computation-unbiased). The two methods stand in exactly the relation
that weighting and standardization stand in throughout causal inference: dual routes to the same estimand,
with complementary assumptions and complementary failure modes.

The setting is the anchored triangle of Chapter 14. An IPD trial, the *index* trial, compares an active
treatment $A$ against a common comparator $C$ in a population $\mathcal P_{AC}$, and supplies the full
covariate, treatment, and outcome record of every patient. A second trial, available only in aggregate, the
*comparator* trial, compares $B$ against the same anchor $C$ in a population $\mathcal P_{BC}$, and supplies
covariate summaries (means $\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$, and where available a covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}$)
together with a published relative effect $\hat d_{BC}$. The clinical question is $A$ versus $B$. As in
Chapter 14 the answer runs through the anchor: estimate the $A$-versus-$C$ effect *in the comparator
population* $\mathcal P_{BC}$, then close the triangle by Bucher's subtraction (@thm-bucher-unbiased). The
entire job of STC is the first step, producing $\hat d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}$, the index trial's relative
effect transported to the comparator population. The bias that this corrects is the transitivity failure of
Chapter 16: the two trials enroll different distributions of effect modifiers (@def-effect-modifier), so the
unadjusted index effect $\hat d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}$ is the right contrast in the wrong population
(@thm-failure-of-bucher).

STC predicts. It fits the conditional mean surface $\mu_k(\mathbf x)=\mathbb E[Y(k)\mid X=\mathbf x]$ on the
index IPD and integrates that surface over the comparator covariate distribution. This is g-computation
with the integrating measure swapped from the source $f_{AC}$ to the target $f_{BC}$, and its validity rests
on conditional transportability of the outcome surface (@thm-conditional-transportability), not on overlap.
A regression can be evaluated wherever its covariates are defined, so STC interpolates and even extrapolates
where MAIC, confined to the convex hull of the IPD (the range of covariate combinations actually observed in
the index trial; @thm-maic-no-extrapolation), cannot. The price is the
mirror image of MAIC's: STC is consistent only if the outcome model is correctly specified, while MAIC needs
no outcome model but relies on a correct weight model or on arm means that are linear in the matched
moments (Chapter 18).

One technical phenomenon dominates the chapter, and it is the phenomenon of Chapter 11:
**non-collapsibility** (@def-non-collapsibility, @thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr). On a non-collapsible link
the *marginal* relative effect a trial reports differs from the relative effect for the *average patient*
(which, under a linear predictor, is also the average of the patients' link-scale effects). STC must therefore choose what it predicts. The historical and
simplest choice, **conditional STC**, plugs the comparator's mean covariate vector $\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$
into the fitted model and reports the effect at that single synthetic patient. We prove that this is biased
for the marginal estimand in general under a nonlinear link (@thm-conditional-stc-bias), with a bias governed by the
curvature of the inverse link and the covariate variance, and that it silently answers a different and
usually unwanted question. The correct choice, **marginal STC**, integrates the fitted means over the
comparator covariate distribution *on the natural outcome scale* and only then applies the link; we prove it
consistent for the marginal effect under correct specification (@thm-marginal-stc-unbiased). A closed-form
counterexample (@thm-stc-noncollapsibility-counterexample) exhibits the gap in a single line of arithmetic,
and a fully worked logistic example (@exm-stc-logistic) carries an STC analysis from a fitted model to three
distinct numbers: the biased plug-in, the correct target marginal, and the unadjusted source marginal.

The plan is as follows. @sec-stc-outcome-model sets up the outcome model and proves the maximum likelihood
estimator (MLE) consistent and asymptotically normal (catalogue G.1), specializing the general theory of
Chapter 5 (@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality). @sec-stc-conditional defines conditional STC and proves its
plug-in bias (G.2). @sec-stc-marginal defines marginal STC, proves its consistency, and identifies it as
transported g-computation (G.3). @sec-stc-noncollapsibility isolates non-collapsibility with a counterexample
and its collapsible boundary (G.4). @sec-stc-example is the worked example. @sec-stc-bayes develops Bayesian
g-computation (G.5). @sec-stc-consistency states the anchored and unanchored STC consistency theorems under
the population-adjustment conditions of Chapter 17 (G.6). @sec-stc-maic-equivalence proves that under a
linear model with first-moment matching MAIC and STC asymptotically coincide (G.7). This chapter corresponds
to results G.1 to G.7 of the proof catalogue. We use the relative-effect notation of [Notation](/notation.qmd)
and the link-position machinery of Chapter 14.

## A concrete picture and the STC workflow {#sec-stc-picture}

The introduction moved fast. Before any formula, fix a picture and keep it for the whole chapter.

**A running clinical example.** A new drug $A$ is to be compared against a competitor drug $B$ for an
autoimmune disease. No trial has ever randomized $A$ directly against $B$. What we have is two separate
randomized trials that share a common comparator, the standard of care $C$:

- the **index trial** $AC$ randomizes $A$ against $C$ and reports **individual patient data (IPD)**: for every
  patient we see the baseline covariates, the assigned arm, and the outcome;
- the **comparator trial** $BC$ randomizes $B$ against $C$ but is published only as **aggregate data (AgD)**:
  covariate summaries (the fraction of patients with each feature) and a single headline effect $\hat d_{BC}$.

Take a single binary covariate $x$, a baseline risk marker, with $x=1$ for a **high-risk** patient and $x=0$
for a **low-risk** patient, and let the outcome be an unfavorable event (a disease flare within six months).
The two trials enrolled different case mixes: the comparator trial $BC$ recruited sicker patients, a fraction
$0.8$ high-risk, against $0.5$ high-risk in the index trial $AC$. Because risk also drives the event
probability, this difference in case mix is precisely what makes a naive indirect comparison invalid; the two
trials answer their questions in two different populations. The numbers in this paragraph are the numbers of
the worked example @exm-stc-logistic, so everything below is a rehearsal for it. The coefficients are chosen
for arithmetic transparency, not clinical realism.

**The anchored triangle.** The three treatments sit at the corners of a triangle. Two edges are supported by
trials; the third, the one we want, is not.

```
     A - - - - - - - - - - - - - B      target: A vs B  (no direct trial)
      \                         /
 A vs C\   AC trial (IPD)      /  BC trial (aggregate)   B vs C
        \                     /
         \                   /
          \                 /
                  C
            common comparator (anchor)
```

STC does exactly one job: it produces the $A$-versus-$C$ effect **evaluated in the comparator population**
$\mathcal P_{BC}$, written $\hat d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}$ (the left edge, transported to the population of the
right edge). Bucher's identity (@thm-bucher-unbiased) then closes the triangle,
$\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\hat d_{BC}$, because both contrasts now refer to the *same*
population $\mathcal P_{BC}$.

**g-computation in two sentences.** STC is the outcome-regression route, called *g-computation* or
*standardization* in Chapter 10 (@thm-g-computation-unbiased). g-computation fits a model for the outcome
given treatment and covariates, then, to get the effect in a chosen population, predicts the outcome for every
covariate profile in that population and averages the predictions. STC is this same recipe with one twist: the
model is fitted in the index population $\mathcal P_{AC}$, but the averaging is done over the *target*
population $\mathcal P_{BC}$.

::: {.remark}
**STC in five steps (the whole method, before the theory).** Given the index IPD and the comparator summaries:

1. **Fit.** Fit an outcome regression $\mu_A(x)$, $\mu_C(x)$ on the index IPD: a model for the event
   probability (or mean) given arm and covariates.
2. **Obtain target covariates.** Get, or reconstruct, the covariate distribution $f_{BC}$ of the comparator
   trial. With IPD this is the covariate table; with only summaries, simulate synthetic patients matching the
   published proportions, means, and (if reported) correlations.
3. **Predict.** For each target covariate profile, use the fitted model to predict the event probability under
   $A$ and under $C$.
4. **Average, then link.** Average those predicted probabilities over the target population *on the natural
   outcome scale* (probabilities, not log odds), and only then convert to the reported effect scale (for
   example the log odds ratio). This order is the crux of the chapter.
5. **Close the triangle.** Combine the resulting $\hat d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}$ with the published
   $\hat d_{BC}$ by Bucher's subtraction (@thm-bucher-unbiased) to get $\hat d_{AB}$.
:::

The single most important warning of the chapter lives in step 4: there are two ways to summarize the fitted
model in the target population, and for a nonlinear outcome model they give *different answers*.

| | **Conditional STC (plug-in)** | **Marginal STC (integrate/simulate)** |
|---|---|---|
| Recipe | plug the target *mean* covariate $\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$ into the fitted model, read off the effect | predict for *every* target covariate profile, average the predictions, then take the effect |
| Order of operations | link, then average (contrast at the average patient) | average, then link (average the outcomes, then contrast) |
| Data needed | only the covariate *means* $\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$ | the full covariate *distribution* $f_{BC}$ |
| Estimand | effect for the single "average patient" (@eq-stc-cond-estimand) | population-average (marginal) effect (@eq-stc-marg-estimand) |
| Correct for a population decision? | under the identity link, and the log link without effect modification; biased in general | yes, under correct specification |
| Developed in | @sec-stc-conditional | @sec-stc-marginal |

The plug-in is historically the original STC of @caro2010stc, and it is tempting for a concrete reason: it
needs only the published covariate *means* $\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$, which every trial reports, not the full
covariate distribution, which most trials do not. Its defect is that "the effect for the average patient" is
not "the average effect" once the outcome model is nonlinear, a phenomenon called **non-collapsibility**
(Chapter 11). Making that gap visible, and fixing it, is the spine of this chapter.

**When to reach for STC.** STC and MAIC (Chapter 18) solve the same transport problem by dual routes, and the
choice between them is a choice of what to trust:

- Reach for **STC** when you are willing to commit to an outcome model (a link and a functional form) and when
  the comparator population lies partly outside the covariate range of the index trial, so that weighting would
  break down. A regression can predict anywhere its covariates are defined.
- Reach for **MAIC** when you do not want to commit to an outcome model and the two populations overlap well,
  so that reweighting is stable. MAIC balances covariate moments and needs no outcome model, though it relies
  on a correct weight model or on arm means linear in the matched moments.

The trade-off, made precise in @sec-stc-maic-equivalence, is "trust a model" (STC) versus "trust an overlap"
(MAIC). Keep it in mind as the assumptions accumulate.

**A guide to the signs and scales.** Two bookkeeping conventions recur and are worth tabulating once. First,
the *direction* of a contrast. The GLM treatment coefficient orients the *active* arm against the *reference*
arm; the relative-effect symbol of [Notation](/notation.qmd) orients the *reference* first. They differ only by
a sign:

| Quantity | Definition | Reads as |
|---|---|---|
| $\Lambda(\mathbf x)$, $\ell_{AC}$ | $\eta_A-\eta_C$ (active minus reference) | GLM/model convention; positive means a higher linear predictor under $A$ |
| $d_{AC(\mathcal P)}$ | $\eta_C-\eta_A$ (reference first) | Notation/Bucher convention; $d_{AC}=-\Lambda$ at the marginal level |

Nothing mathematical depends on the choice; we compute in the positive $\ell_{AC}=\eta_A-\eta_C$ where it keeps
arithmetic tidy and flip the sign only when handing the result to Bucher. Second, the *scale*. Every effect can
be read on two scales, and the whole non-collapsibility story is that they do not commute with averaging:

| Phrase (used interchangeably) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **natural outcome scale** = response scale | the untransformed outcome: an event *probability*, a *rate*, a mean |
| **link scale** | the transformed outcome $g(\cdot)$: a *log odds*, a *log rate*, on which the model is linear |

We say "natural outcome scale" for the untransformed scale throughout. "Averaging on the natural outcome scale,
then linking" is marginal STC; "linking, then reading the contrast at the average covariate" is conditional
STC. Finally, a compact glossary of the symbols this chapter leans on, all consistent with
[Notation](/notation.qmd):

| Symbol | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| $\mathcal P_{AC}$, $\mathcal P_{BC}$ | source (index) and target (comparator) populations |
| $f_{BC}$ | covariate distribution in the target population |
| $\eta_k(\mathbf x)$ | linear predictor (link-scale outcome) under arm $k$ |
| $\mu_k(\mathbf x)$ | fitted event probability or mean under arm $k$, on the natural outcome scale |
| $\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}$ | that mean, *averaged* over population $\mathcal P$ (a marginal mean) |
| $d^{\mathrm{cond}}$ | conditional-at-the-mean effect (the plug-in target) |
| $d^{\mathrm{marg}}$ | marginal (population-average) effect (the correct target) |
| $\Lambda(\mathbf x)$ | conditional relative effect on the link scale, $\gamma+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2$ |

With the picture, the workflow, the two estimands, and the bookkeeping in hand, we now build the method
rigorously, beginning with the regression that step 1 fits.

## The outcome model and its estimation {#sec-stc-outcome-model}

This section carries out step 1 of the workflow: fitting the outcome regression. Why begin with a page of
maximum likelihood theory in a chapter about STC? Because *every* downstream STC estimator, the plug-in of
@sec-stc-conditional, the marginal estimator of @sec-stc-marginal, and their variances, is a function of the
fitted coefficients $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$. To push convergence and a limiting distribution through those
functions we need two guarantees about $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ itself: that it converges to the truth
(consistency) and that it has a known limiting spread (asymptotic normality). @thm-stc-outcome-mle supplies
both; the reader who trusts that GLMs are well behaved may skim its proof and rejoin at @sec-stc-conditional.

Fix a strictly increasing, twice continuously differentiable link function $g$ (@def-link-function) with
inverse $g^{-1}$: the logit for binary outcomes, the log for rates and hazards, the identity for continuous
outcomes. The index IPD consist of $n$ independent records $(Y_i, T_i, \mathbf x_i)$, $i=1,\dots,n$, drawn
from $\mathcal P_{AC}$, with arm indicator $T_i\in\{A,C\}$ randomized and covariates
$\mathbf x_i\in\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^p$.

::: {#def-stc-outcome-model}
## The STC outcome model
The **outcome model** is the generalized linear model that, with $C$ as the reference arm, writes the
conditional mean of the outcome on the link scale as a linear predictor
$$
\eta_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)
\;=\;\alpha \;+\; \mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1 \;+\; \mathbf 1\{k=A\}\,\bigl(\gamma+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2\bigr),
\qquad k\in\{A,C\},
$$ {#eq-stc-linpred}
with intercept $\alpha$, prognostic coefficients $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ (@def-prognostic-variable), treatment
main effect $\gamma$, and treatment-by-covariate interactions $\boldsymbol\beta_2$ encoding effect
modification (@def-effect-modifier). The full parameter is $\boldsymbol\xi=(\alpha,\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2)\in\mathbb R^{q}$,
$q=2p+2$. The **fitted conditional mean** under arm $k$ is
$$
\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)\;=\;g^{-1}\!\bigl(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)\bigr),
\qquad
\mu_k(\mathbf x)\;:=\;\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi_0)\;=\;\mathbb E[Y(k)\mid X=\mathbf x],
$$ {#eq-stc-condmean}
the last equality holding at the true parameter $\boldsymbol\xi_0$ under correct specification. The
**conditional relative effect** of $A$ versus $C$ at covariate value $\mathbf x$ is the contrast of linear
predictors,
$$
\Lambda(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)\;=\;\eta_A(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)-\eta_C(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)\;=\;\gamma+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2 .
$$ {#eq-stc-cate-link}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader's translation.* The model says that each patient's outcome, on the link scale, is a baseline level
($\alpha$), plus a prognostic tilt for how sick they are ($\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1$), plus, only if
they received the active drug, a treatment bump ($\gamma$) that may itself depend on their covariates
($\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2$, effect modification). Set $\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0$ and every patient
gets the same treatment bump; let it be nonzero and the drug helps some patients more than others. The
conditional relative effect @eq-stc-cate-link is just that treatment bump on the link scale.

Writing $z_i=\bigl(1,\ \mathbf 1\{T_i=A\},\ \mathbf x_i^\top,\ \mathbf 1\{T_i=A\}\,\mathbf x_i^\top\bigr)^\top\in\mathbb R^{q}$
for the design row of patient $i$, the linear predictor is $\eta_i=z_i^\top\boldsymbol\xi$, so
@eq-stc-linpred is an ordinary GLM with model matrix $Z=[z_1,\dots,z_n]^\top$. The conditional relative
effect @eq-stc-cate-link is constant in $\mathbf x$ exactly when $\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0$, that is,
when no measured covariate modifies the treatment effect on the link scale; this is the link-scale form of
the effect-modifier definition of Chapter 11.

::: {.remark}
**Orientation of the contrast.** Equation @eq-stc-cate-link is the effect of the *active* arm relative to
the *reference* arm, $\eta_A-\eta_C$, which is the sign convention of the GLM treatment coefficient and of
the STC literature. The relative-effect symbol of [Notation](/notation.qmd) and Chapter 14 places the
reference first, $d_{AC(\mathcal P)}=\eta_{C(\mathcal P)}-\eta_{A(\mathcal P)}$, so the marginal version of
@eq-stc-cate-link enters Bucher's identity as $d_{AC}=-\Lambda$ at the marginal level. The overall sign is
bookkeeping, exactly as in the index-order remark of Chapter 14, and it changes none of the bias,
consistency, or non-collapsibility statements below, each of which is a statement about a single arm or about
the difference of two arms on a fixed scale. To keep the worked arithmetic in positive numbers we report the
active-versus-reference log odds-ratio $\ell_{AC}:=\eta_{A}-\eta_{C}$ where convenient and note
$d_{AC}=-\ell_{AC}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### Estimation and its large-sample behavior {#sec-stc-mle}

The model is fitted by maximum likelihood. For an outcome whose conditional law is a one-parameter
exponential-family member with mean $\mu_i=g^{-1}(z_i^\top\boldsymbol\xi)$, the log-likelihood is
$$
\ell_n(\boldsymbol\xi)\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi),
\qquad
\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi)=\frac{Y_i\vartheta_i-b(\vartheta_i)}{a(\phi)}+c(Y_i,\phi),
$$ {#eq-stc-loglik}
where $\vartheta_i$ is the natural parameter, related to the mean by $\mu_i=b'(\vartheta_i)$ and to the
linear predictor by the link $g(\mu_i)=z_i^\top\boldsymbol\xi$, and $a(\phi)>0$ is the dispersion. The score
and observed information are
$$
\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\xi)=\nabla\ell_n(\boldsymbol\xi)=\sum_i \frac{Y_i-\mu_i}{a(\phi)\,V(\mu_i)\,g'(\mu_i)}\,z_i,
\qquad
\mathcal I_n(\boldsymbol\xi)=\sum_i W_i\,z_iz_i^\top,
$$ {#eq-stc-score}
with variance function $V(\mu)=b''(\vartheta)$ and GLM working weight
$W_i=\bigl[a(\phi)\,V(\mu_i)\,g'(\mu_i)^2\bigr]^{-1}>0$ (the standard iteratively reweighted least squares
weight; see @mccullagh1989glm, Chapter 2). We record the asymptotics as catalogue result G.1.

::: {#thm-stc-outcome-mle}
## Consistency and asymptotic normality of the outcome MLE
Suppose the outcome model @def-stc-outcome-model is correctly specified, with true parameter
$\boldsymbol\xi_0$ in the interior of a compact parameter set $\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^{q}$, and that

1. the records $(Y_i,T_i,\mathbf x_i)$ are independent and identically distributed from $\mathcal P_{AC}$,
   with $\mathbb E[Y(k)\mid X=\mathbf x]=g^{-1}(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi_0))$;
2. the covariates are bounded and the limiting design second moment
   $\mathbf M:=\mathbb E[\,W\,zz^\top\,]$ is finite and positive definite, which requires both arms to be
   present with positive probability and the covariates to vary within the active arm so that the columns of
   $z$ corresponding to $\alpha,\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta_1,\boldsymbol\beta_2$ are not collinear;
3. the link $g$ is twice continuously differentiable with $g'>0$, and the dispersion $a(\phi)$ is fixed or
   estimated by a $\sqrt n$-consistent estimator.

Then the maximum likelihood estimator $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ exists with probability tending to one, is
consistent, $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\xi_0$, and is asymptotically normal,
$$
\sqrt n\,(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}-\boldsymbol\xi_0)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \mathcal N\!\bigl(\mathbf 0,\ \mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^{-1}\bigr),
\qquad
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)=\mathbf M,
$$ {#eq-stc-mle-an}
where $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)$ is the per-observation Fisher information. (Corresponds to G.1 in the
proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
The result is the master maximum likelihood theorem of Chapter 5 (@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality) applied to
the estimating function @eq-stc-score; the work is to verify its hypotheses for the GLM @eq-stc-loglik. We
take $a(\phi)$ known to lighten notation; a $\sqrt n$-consistent $\hat\phi$ enters the mean parameters only
through a block-diagonal information and does not change the limit for $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$.

*Identifiability.* The map $\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto(\eta_1,\dots,\eta_n)=(z_1^\top\boldsymbol\xi,\dots)$ is
injective on $\mathbb R^q$ iff the design rows span $\mathbb R^q$, equivalently iff
$\mathbb E[zz^\top]\succ0$. Hypothesis 2 grants this: an intercept needs a constant column; $\gamma$ needs
$\Pr(T=A)\in(0,1)$ so the column $\mathbf 1\{T=A\}$ is nonconstant; $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ needs covariate
variation; $\boldsymbol\beta_2$ needs covariate variation within the active arm. Since $g$ is strictly
increasing, distinct linear predictors give distinct mean vectors, so distinct $\boldsymbol\xi$ give distinct
distributions and the parameter is identified.

*The score has mean zero at the truth.* Under correct specification, $\mathbb E[Y_i\mid z_i]=\mu_i(\boldsymbol\xi_0)$,
so each summand of @eq-stc-score has conditional mean
$$
\mathbb E\!\left[\frac{Y_i-\mu_i(\boldsymbol\xi_0)}{a(\phi)V(\mu_i)g'(\mu_i)}\,z_i\ \middle|\ z_i\right]=\mathbf 0,
$$
and hence unconditional mean zero by the tower property (the law of iterated expectations,
$\mathbb E[\mathbb E[Y\mid X]]=\mathbb E[Y]$). Thus $\boldsymbol\xi_0$ solves the population score
equation $\mathbb E[\mathbf s_i(\boldsymbol\xi_0)]=\mathbf 0$, the defining property of the estimand for an
M-estimator (an estimator defined as the zero of an estimating function, here the score $\mathbf s_n$).

*Information and the second-moment matrix.* Differentiating @eq-stc-score and taking expectations, the
cross-product terms in $Y_i-\mu_i$ vanish in expectation at $\boldsymbol\xi_0$, leaving the Fisher
information per observation
$$
\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)=\mathbb E\!\left[-\nabla^2\ell_i(\boldsymbol\xi_0)\right]=\mathbb E\!\left[\,W_i\,z_iz_i^\top\,\right]=\mathbf M,
$$
which is finite (bounded covariates, continuous weights) and positive definite by hypothesis 2 together with
$W_i>0$. This is the information equality for a correctly specified exponential family.

*Existence, uniqueness, and consistency.* For the canonical link the log-likelihood @eq-stc-loglik is
concave in $\boldsymbol\xi$ because $b$ is convex and $\eta_i$ is linear in $\boldsymbol\xi$, so any
stationary point is the unique global maximizer; for a noncanonical but smooth strictly increasing link the
log-likelihood is locally concave near $\boldsymbol\xi_0$ and the estimating function $\mathbf s_n$ is, by
the uniform law of large numbers on the compact $\Xi$, uniformly close to its expectation, whose unique
zero is $\boldsymbol\xi_0$. By the standard M-estimation consistency argument (the zero of an estimating
function that converges uniformly to a function with a well-separated unique zero is consistent;
@vandervaart1998, Theorem 5.9), $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\xi_0$.

*Asymptotic normality.* A first-order Taylor expansion of $\mathbf 0=\mathbf s_n(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})$ about
$\boldsymbol\xi_0$ gives
$$
\mathbf 0=\frac1{\sqrt n}\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\xi_0)+\Bigl(\frac1n\nabla\mathbf s_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol\xi})\Bigr)\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}-\boldsymbol\xi_0),
$$
for $\tilde{\boldsymbol\xi}$ on the segment between $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ and $\boldsymbol\xi_0$. The score
summands are independent, mean zero, with per-observation covariance $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)=\mathbf M$
(the information equality), so by the multivariate central limit theorem
$n^{-1/2}\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\xi_0)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf M)$. By consistency and the
uniform law of large numbers $-n^{-1}\nabla\mathbf s_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol\xi})\xrightarrow{p}\mathbf M$ (the
observed information per observation converging to the Fisher information $\mathbf M$), which
is invertible. Solving for $\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}-\boldsymbol\xi_0)$ and applying Slutsky's theorem,
$$
\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}-\boldsymbol\xi_0)=\mathbf M^{-1}\,\frac1{\sqrt n}\mathbf s_n(\boldsymbol\xi_0)+o_p(1)\ \xrightarrow{d}\ \mathcal N\!\bigl(\mathbf 0,\ \mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf M\,\mathbf M^{-1}\bigr)=\mathcal N\!\bigl(\mathbf 0,\ \mathbf M^{-1}\bigr),
$$
which is @eq-stc-mle-an. The sandwich form $\mathbf M^{-1}\mathbf M\mathbf M^{-1}$ collapses to
$\mathbf M^{-1}$ precisely because correct specification forces the meat to equal the bread. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** Every STC estimator in this chapter, the plug-in, the marginal estimator, and their
delta-method and Bayesian variances, is a function of $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$. @thm-stc-outcome-mle is what lets
us carry convergence and a limiting distribution *through* those functions: consistency of $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$
becomes consistency of the transported effect (@thm-marginal-stc-unbiased), and the Gaussian limit becomes the
standard error we report. It is the same relationship regression has to everything built on it: pin down the
coefficients first, then read off whatever functional the application needs.

::: {.remark}
**Misspecification and the sandwich.** Drop hypothesis 1. The estimating function @eq-stc-score still has a
well-defined zero $\boldsymbol\xi^\ast$, the **pseudo-true parameter**, solving
$\mathbb E[\mathbf s_i(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)]=\mathbf 0$; it minimizes the Kullback-Leibler divergence from the
true law to the model family (@vandervaart1998, Section 5.5). The same Taylor argument then yields
$\sqrt n(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}-\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\ \mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf B\mathbf A^{-1})$,
the **sandwich** of @def-sandwich-variance, with bread $\mathbf A=\mathbb E[-\nabla\mathbf s_i(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)]$
and meat $\mathbf B=\mathbb E[\mathbf s_i(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)\mathbf s_i(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)^\top]$, which no
longer coincide. The estimator is then consistent for $\boldsymbol\xi^\ast$, not $\boldsymbol\xi_0$, and the
STC contrasts built from it inherit a bias equal to the discrepancy between the pseudo-true surface and the
truth. This is the formal statement of STC's central vulnerability: it is only as good as its model.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**A misspecification example.** Suppose the true event probability rises with the *square* of a covariate,
$\operatorname{logit}\mu_C(x)=-1+x^2$, but the analyst fits the straight-line model
$\operatorname{logit}\mu_C(x)=\alpha+\beta_1 x$. Inside the index covariate range the straight line can track
the curve tolerably, so the fit looks fine on the data at hand. But STC's selling point is that it
*extrapolates* into the comparator population, and where that population places patients at larger $x$ than the
index trial ever observed, the straight line and the true parabola diverge without bound. STC then transports a
confident prediction that is simply wrong: the pseudo-true surface $\mu_k(\cdot;\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)$ is not the
truth off the index support, and the transported contrast inherits exactly that error. This is why "no overlap
required" (@sec-stc-marginal below) is a statement about mathematical definability, not a license to
extrapolate blindly. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Conditional simulated treatment comparison and its plug-in bias {#sec-stc-conditional}

The fitted model can be queried in two essentially different ways, and the difference is the subject of the
chapter. The first, historically the original STC of @caro2010stc, evaluates the fitted contrast at a single
synthetic patient whose covariates equal the comparator-population mean.

::: {#def-stc-conditional}
## Conditional (plug-in) STC
Given the fitted model $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ and the comparator covariate mean $\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$, the
**conditional STC estimator** of the $A$-versus-$C$ relative effect is the fitted conditional relative
effect @eq-stc-cate-link evaluated at $\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$,
$$
\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}
\;:=\; g\!\bigl(\mu_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC};\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\bigr)-g\!\bigl(\mu_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC};\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\bigr)
\;=\;\eta_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC};\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})-\eta_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC};\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})
\;=\;-\bigl(\hat\gamma+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_2\bigr),
$$ {#eq-stc-cond}
in the reference-first orientation of [Notation](/notation.qmd). It is the relative effect predicted for an
individual whose covariate vector equals the comparator mean. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader's translation.* Conditional STC builds one synthetic "average patient," whose covariates are the
target-population means, and reports the treatment effect the model predicts for that single patient. It was
the original proposal of @caro2010stc for a blunt practical reason: it needs only the published covariate
*means* $\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$, which every trial reports, and never the full covariate distribution, which most
trials do not. The rest of this section shows what that convenience costs.

The middle equality in @eq-stc-cond is exact and not an approximation: applying the link $g$ to a fitted
conditional mean returns the linear predictor, $g(\mu_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}))=\eta_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})$,
because $\mu_k=g^{-1}\circ\eta_k$. The conditional estimator is therefore a difference of *linear*
predictors, and it inherits no curvature. That is exactly the trouble: the marginal estimand it is meant to
approximate is a difference of links of *averaged* means, which does carry curvature. We isolate the target.

::: {#def-stc-estimands}
## The marginal and conditional-at-the-mean estimands
Let $\mathcal P$ be a population with covariate density $f_{\mathcal P}$, and write the arm marginal mean and
its link-scale position, as in @eq-bucher-eta of Chapter 14,
$$
\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}=\int \mu_k(\mathbf x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x,
\qquad
\eta_{k(\mathcal P)}=g\!\bigl(\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-stc-armmean}
The **marginal relative effect** in $\mathcal P$ is the contrast of link positions (@def-marginal-effect),
$$
d_{AC(\mathcal P)}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\;=\;\eta_{C(\mathcal P)}-\eta_{A(\mathcal P)}\;=\;g\!\bigl(\bar\mu_{C(\mathcal P)}\bigr)-g\!\bigl(\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal P)}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-stc-marg-estimand}
and the **conditional-at-the-mean** effect is the link contrast at the mean covariate (@def-conditional-effect),
$$
d_{AC(\mathcal P)}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}\;=\;g\!\bigl(\mu_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P})\bigr)-g\!\bigl(\mu_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P})\bigr)\;=\;\eta_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P})-\eta_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P}).
$$ {#eq-stc-cond-estimand}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader's translation: the average of outcomes versus the outcome of the average.* The **marginal** effect
@eq-stc-marg-estimand averages the outcomes and *then* contrasts (what a trial run in $\mathcal P$ would
report); the **conditional-at-the-mean** effect @eq-stc-cond-estimand contrasts at the single average patient.
A straight-line model makes the two equal; a curved link splits them, and a population-level decision wants the
first.

The marginal effect @eq-stc-marg-estimand is the quantity a randomized trial in $\mathcal P$ would report
from its arm summaries, and the quantity Bucher's identity requires (@def-constancy-relative-effects). The
conditional-at-the-mean effect @eq-stc-cond-estimand is the effect for a single hypothetical average patient.
The conditional STC estimator @eq-stc-cond is consistent for @eq-stc-cond-estimand, by @thm-stc-outcome-mle
and the continuity of $g\circ g^{-1}$, but for the marginal estimand it carries a bias that we now compute
exactly. The result is catalogue G.2.

The intuition is one sentence: *a curved link makes the prediction at the mean covariate differ from the mean
of the predictions.* Bend a curve, mark the midpoint of two inputs, and the curve's height at that midpoint is
not the average of its two output heights; the gap grows with how much the curve bends and how spread out the
inputs are. The next theorem turns that sentence into an exact formula: the arm-level gap is, to second order,
half the variance of the linear predictor times the curvature of the inverse link (@eq-stc-taylor).

::: {#thm-conditional-stc-bias}
## Plug-in bias of conditional STC under a nonlinear link
Assume the outcome model @def-stc-outcome-model is correctly specified and that $g^{-1}$ is twice
differentiable on the range of the linear predictors. Then:

1. **What it estimates.** $\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}\xrightarrow{p} d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}$,
   the conditional-at-the-mean effect @eq-stc-cond-estimand, not the marginal effect.

2. **Arm-level Jensen gap.** For each arm $k$ the link of the marginal mean differs from the linear
   predictor at the mean by
   $$
   \eta_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})
   = g\!\bigl(\mathbb E_{f_{BC}}[\mu_k(X)]\bigr)-g\!\bigl(\mu_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})\bigr),
   $$ {#eq-stc-armgap}
   and, writing $b_k:=\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\mu_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})=\mathbb E_{f_{BC}}[\mu_k(X)]-\mu_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})$
   for the response-scale gap,
   $$
   b_k=\tfrac12\,\mathbb E_{f_{BC}}\!\Bigl[\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top(X-\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})\bigr)^2\,(g^{-1})''(\xi_{k,X})\Bigr],
   \qquad \boldsymbol\beta_{(C)}=\boldsymbol\beta_1,\ \boldsymbol\beta_{(A)}=\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2,
   $$ {#eq-stc-taylor}
   for some $\xi_{k,X}$ between $\eta_k(X)$ and $\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})$. The gap $b_k$ is nonzero
   whenever $(g^{-1})''$ is nonzero with constant sign on the relevant range and
   $\mathrm{Var}_{f_{BC}}(\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top X)>0$.

3. **Contrast bias.** The asymptotic bias of conditional STC for the marginal effect is the difference of
   the two arm-level link gaps @eq-stc-armgap,
      $$
   d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}-d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}
   =\bigl[\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\eta_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})\bigr]-\bigl[\eta_{C(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\eta_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})\bigr],
   $$ {#eq-stc-contrastbias}
   which vanishes for the identity link and is generally nonzero otherwise.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1 (what the plug-in converges to).* By @thm-stc-outcome-mle, $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\xi_0$, and the maps
$\boldsymbol\xi\mapsto\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC};\boldsymbol\xi)$ are continuous (indeed affine), so by the
continuous mapping theorem$\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}=\eta_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC};\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})-\eta_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC};\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\xrightarrow{p}\eta_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})-\eta_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}$,
which is @eq-stc-cond-estimand by definition.

*Part 2 (the per-arm Jensen gap).* Fix an arm $k$ and abbreviate $\eta_k(\mathbf x)=\eta_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi_0)$,
$m(\mathbf x)=\mu_k(\mathbf x)=g^{-1}(\eta_k(\mathbf x))$, $\bar{\mathbf x}=\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$. Because
$\eta_k$ is affine, $\eta_k(X)-\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x})=\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top(X-\bar{\mathbf x})$ with
$\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}$ the covariate slope of arm $k$, namely $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ for $C$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2$ for $A$. A second-order Taylor expansion of $m=g^{-1}\circ\eta_k$
about $\bar{\mathbf x}$ with Lagrange remainder gives, for each $\mathbf x$,
$$
m(\mathbf x)=m(\bar{\mathbf x})+(g^{-1})'(\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x}))\,\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x})+\tfrac12(g^{-1})''(\xi_{k,\mathbf x})\,\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top(\mathbf x-\bar{\mathbf x})\bigr)^2,
$$
with $\xi_{k,\mathbf x}$ between $\eta_k(\mathbf x)$ and $\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x})$. Take the expectation over
$X\sim f_{BC}$. The first term is constant; the second term vanishes because
$\mathbb E_{f_{BC}}[X-\bar{\mathbf x}]=\mathbf 0$ and the coefficient is constant; the third term gives
@eq-stc-taylor:
$$
b_k=\mathbb E_{f_{BC}}[m(X)]-m(\bar{\mathbf x})=\tfrac12\,\mathbb E_{f_{BC}}\!\Bigl[(g^{-1})''(\xi_{k,X})\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top(X-\bar{\mathbf x})\bigr)^2\Bigr].
$$
The integrand is a product of $(g^{-1})''$ and a nonnegative quadratic with positive expectation when the
slope contrast has positive variance; if moreover $(g^{-1})''$ has a constant sign on the range (true for the
logit on either side of zero and for the log everywhere), the gap $b_k$ is strictly of that sign, hence
nonzero. Applying the increasing function $g$ to the two means in @eq-stc-armmean and subtracting gives the
link-scale gap @eq-stc-armgap, which is a strictly monotone transform of $b_k$ and therefore vanishes iff
$b_k=0$.

*Part 3 (the contrast bias is the difference of the two gaps).* Subtract the marginal estimand @eq-stc-marg-estimand from the conditional-at-the-mean estimand
@eq-stc-cond-estimand and regroup by arm:
$$
\begin{aligned}
d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}-d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}
&=\bigl[\eta_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})-\eta_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})\bigr]-\bigl[\eta_{C(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{BC})}\bigr]\\
&=\bigl[\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\eta_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})\bigr]-\bigl[\eta_{C(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\eta_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})\bigr],
\end{aligned}
$$
which is @eq-stc-contrastbias. For the identity link $g^{-1}(\eta)=\eta$, so $(g^{-1})''\equiv0$ and each
$b_k=0$ by @eq-stc-taylor, hence each bracket in @eq-stc-contrastbias vanishes and the contrast bias is zero.
For a nonlinear link the two brackets are the arm-level gaps @eq-stc-armgap, which are individually nonzero
and need not cancel, so the contrast bias is generally nonzero. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** A cost-effectiveness model, the engine of a health technology assessment, is handed a
*single* marginal effect together with a target population, and it prices a technology for that whole
population. Feed it the conditional-at-the-mean effect instead and you have silently evaluated the drug for one
hypothetical average patient, not for the population the funding decision actually covers. @thm-conditional-stc-bias
says the substitution is not a rounding error: under a non-collapsible link, and under the log link
whenever there is effect modification, it is a systematic bias, invisible
without the covariate distribution and unshrinkable by collecting more data (it is a bias, not a variance).
This is why STC, and its descendant ML-NMR (Chapter 20), integrate on the natural outcome scale rather than
plug in a mean.

The decomposition @eq-stc-contrastbias is the precise content of the slogan "the link does not commute with
averaging." It also shows *exactly when conditional STC happens to be unbiased for the marginal effect*: not
only under the identity link, but whenever the two arm-level Jensen gaps coincide. The log link makes this
boundary explicit and connects it to collapsibility.

::: {#exm-stc-loglink}
## The log link: exact bias and the collapsibility of the rate ratio
Let $g=\log$, so $g^{-1}(\eta)=e^{\eta}$ and $(g^{-1})''=e^{\eta}>0$ everywhere, and let
$X\sim\mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC},\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC})$ in the comparator population. By the moment
generating function of the multivariate Gaussian (Chapter 4), for each arm
$$
\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\mathbb E[e^{\eta_k(X)}]=\exp\!\Bigl(\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})+\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}\Bigr),
$$
so the arm link gap @eq-stc-armgap is the exact constant
$\eta_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC})=\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}>0$.
The plug-in underestimates each arm's marginal mean by the multiplicative factor
$e^{\frac12\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}}>1$. The contrast bias
@eq-stc-contrastbias is therefore the exact quantity
$$
d^{\,\mathrm{cond}}-d^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=\tfrac12\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2\bigr)^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_2\bigr)-\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_1
=\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2+\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_2^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2.
$$
This vanishes exactly when $\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0$, that is, when no covariate modifies the treatment
effect: under the log link the two arm gaps are equal whenever the arm slopes are equal, and the contrast is
**collapsible** even though each arm separately suffers a nonzero plug-in gap. The rate ratio and risk ratio
are collapsible in exactly this sense (@def-collapsibility). The logit link enjoys no such cancellation, as
the next section's counterexample shows: the odds ratio is non-collapsible, and conditional STC is biased for
the marginal log odds ratio even with $\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**A legitimate estimand for the wrong question.** The conditional-at-the-mean effect @eq-stc-cond-estimand is
not a mistake of definition; it is a well-defined quantity, the effect a clinician would quote for a patient
whose covariates sit at the population average. Its defect is one of *fitness for purpose*. A health
technology assessment compares two treatments at the level of a whole population, and the population-level
contrast is the marginal effect @eq-stc-marg-estimand, the average of outcomes, not the outcome of the
average. Reporting @eq-stc-cond-estimand where @eq-stc-marg-estimand is wanted substitutes one estimand for
another and, by @thm-conditional-stc-bias, does so with a bias that is invisible without the covariate
distribution. The defect is also not removed by a larger sample: it is a bias, not a variance.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Marginal simulated treatment comparison {#sec-stc-marginal}

The cure is to integrate before linking. Marginal STC averages the fitted conditional means over the
comparator covariate distribution *on the natural outcome scale*, and applies the link only to the resulting
marginal means.

::: {#def-stc-marginal}
## Marginal STC
With the fitted model $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ and a sample (or density) representing the comparator covariate
distribution $f_{BC}$, the **marginal STC predicted means** under the two arms are
$$
\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}}=\int \mu_A(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x,
\qquad
\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{STC}}=\int \mu_C(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x,
$$ {#eq-stc-marg-mean}
and the **marginal STC estimator** of the relative effect is their link contrast
$$
\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\;=\;g\!\bigl(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{STC}}\bigr)-g\!\bigl(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-stc-marg}
In practice the integrals @eq-stc-marg-mean are Monte Carlo averages over $M$ covariate vectors
$\{\mathbf x_s^\ast\}_{s=1}^M$ drawn from $f_{BC}$, or over the observed AgD patient covariates when those are
available,
$$
\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}\;\approx\;\frac1M\sum_{s=1}^M \mu_k(\mathbf x_s^\ast;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}).
$$ {#eq-stc-mc}
When only marginal covariate summaries are published, $f_{BC}$ is reconstructed from a parametric model,
typically a Gaussian copula (Chapter 22), before sampling. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader's translation: this is where the "simulation" happens.* The integral @eq-stc-marg-mean is almost never
available in closed form for a nonlinear model, so in practice we *simulate*: draw $M$ synthetic patients from
the target covariate distribution $f_{BC}$, push each through the fitted model to get their predicted event
probabilities under $A$ and $C$, and average @eq-stc-mc. That averaging is the "simulated" in *simulated
treatment comparison*. We are not simulating outcomes, nor a missing trial arm; we are numerically averaging
fitted predictions over a target case mix.

::: {.remark}
**Simulating covariates from aggregate data.** When the comparator trial reports patient-level covariates,
$f_{BC}$ *is* those patients and step 2 is trivial. When it reports only summaries, we must *reconstruct*
$f_{BC}$ before we can sample it, and how much we can reconstruct depends on what was published:

- *Only proportions and means.* A binary covariate is reproduced exactly from its reported prevalence; a
  continuous covariate is reproduced from a reported mean and standard deviation under an assumed shape (often
  Gaussian). With no reported correlations, the covariates are simulated as *independent*, which is itself an
  assumption.
- *Means, variances, and a correlation matrix.* The joint distribution can be reconstructed with a copula
  (Chapter 22; see [Notation](/notation.qmd)), typically a Gaussian copula, which glues the reported margins
  together with the reported correlations.
- *Impossible combinations.* A naive independent simulation can generate covariate profiles that never occur
  clinically (for example a pregnant male, or an implausible age-comorbidity pairing); realistic dependence, or
  explicit constraints, are needed to avoid predicting the fitted model into nonsense regions.

The reconstructed $f_{BC}$ is an *input*, not a fact: if it is wrong, marginal STC integrates the fitted
surface over the wrong measure and is biased even when the outcome model is perfect. This dependence on a
reconstructed covariate distribution is a distinct source of uncertainty, listed in the checklist of
@sec-stc-bayes. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The order of operations in @eq-stc-marg is the whole point, and it is the order of g-computation. We make
that identification precise, then prove consistency.

::: {#prp-stc-gcomp}
## Marginal STC is transported g-computation
The marginal STC predicted means @eq-stc-marg-mean are the g-computation (standardization) functionals of
Chapter 10 with the integrating measure set to the *target* covariate distribution $f_{BC}$ rather than the
source $f_{AC}$. If, in addition to correct specification, the conditional outcome surface is transportable,
$\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_{BC}}[Y(k)\mid X=\mathbf x]=\mu_k(\mathbf x)$ for $f_{BC}$-almost every $\mathbf x$
(@thm-conditional-transportability), then $\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_{BC}}[Y(k)]$,
the marginal potential-outcome mean of arm $k$ in the comparator population.
:::

::: {.proof}
The g-computation functional for arm $k$ in a population $\mathcal P$ is, by @thm-g-computation-unbiased,
$\int\mu_k(\mathbf x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x=\mathbb E_{\mathcal P}[Y(k)]$ under consistency,
ignorability, and a correct $\mu_k$. Equation @eq-stc-marg-mean is this functional evaluated with
$f_{\mathcal P}=f_{BC}$ and the source-fitted surface $\mu_k(\cdot;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})$. The surface is
identified from the index trial, where arm $A$ is observed; transportability (@thm-conditional-transportability,
the population-adjustment instance of @def-transportability) asserts that this same surface governs the
conditional means in the comparator population, where arm $A$ is unobserved. Under that assumption the tower
property gives
$\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_{BC}}[Y(k)]=\mathbb E_{f_{BC}}\bigl[\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_{BC}}[Y(k)\mid X]\bigr]=\mathbb E_{f_{BC}}[\mu_k(X)]=\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}$.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why STC needs no overlap.** The g-computation identity requires only that $\mu_k(\cdot)$ be the correct and
transportable conditional surface; it places no positivity requirement on $f_{BC}$ relative to $f_{AC}$. The
integral @eq-stc-marg-mean can be evaluated at covariate values the index trial never observed, because a
regression returns a prediction wherever its predictors are defined. This is precisely the property that
inverse-probability weighting, and therefore MAIC, lacks (@thm-maic-no-extrapolation): a weight is undefined
where the source density is zero. STC trades the overlap requirement for an extrapolation that is only as
trustworthy as the model is correct off the support of $f_{AC}$. Read those two words carefully: STC's freedom
from overlap is a statement about mathematical *definability*, not scientific *credibility*. A regression will
always return a number outside the index covariate range, but that number rests entirely on the model's assumed
functional form there, which the data cannot check (recall the misspecification example after
@thm-stc-outcome-mle). Good practice therefore diagnoses and reports the extent of extrapolation, for instance
by flagging how much of the target covariate distribution falls outside the index trial's observed range,
exactly the region where MAIC would refuse to weight and STC quietly predicts anyway. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-marginal-stc-unbiased}
## Consistency of marginal STC
Assume (i) the outcome model @def-stc-outcome-model is correctly specified, so $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\xi_0$
by @thm-stc-outcome-mle; (ii) the conditional outcome surface is transportable to the comparator population
(@prp-stc-gcomp); and (iii) the integrals @eq-stc-marg-mean are computed exactly, or by Monte Carlo
@eq-stc-mc with $M\to\infty$. Then the marginal STC predicted means and the marginal STC estimator are
consistent,
$$
\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}\xrightarrow{p}\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_{BC}}[Y(k)],
\qquad
\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\xrightarrow{p} d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}},
$$ {#eq-stc-marg-consistency}
the marginal relative effect @eq-stc-marg-estimand of $A$ versus $C$ in the comparator population.
(Corresponds to G.3 in the proof catalogue.)

[machine-checked: `theories/STC.v`, `Theorem STC_consistent`]
:::

::: {.proof}
Fix an arm $k$. The fitted conditional mean is $\mu_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})=g^{-1}(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}))$,
a composition of the continuous $g^{-1}$ with the affine $\eta_k(\mathbf x;\cdot)$. Since
$\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\xi_0$ and the covariates are bounded (hypothesis 2 of
@thm-stc-outcome-mle), the convergence is uniform over the bounded covariate range: for any $\epsilon>0$,
$\sup_{\mathbf x}\,|\mu_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})-\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi_0)|\xrightarrow{p}0$,
because $g^{-1}$ is uniformly continuous on the compact image of the linear predictor and the affine map is
jointly continuous. Integrating against the probability measure $f_{BC}$ preserves the uniform bound,
$$
\Bigl|\,\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}-\textstyle\int\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi_0)f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\,\Bigr|
\le \sup_{\mathbf x}\bigl|\mu_k(\mathbf x;\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})-\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi_0)\bigr|\xrightarrow{p}0,
$$
so $\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}\xrightarrow{p}\int\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi_0)f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x=\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}$.
By @prp-stc-gcomp this limit equals $\mathbb E_{\mathcal P_{BC}}[Y(k)]$, the transported potential-outcome
mean. When the integral is replaced by the Monte Carlo average @eq-stc-mc, the strong law of large numbers
gives $\frac1M\sum_s\mu_k(\mathbf x_s^\ast;\boldsymbol\xi)\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}$
for each fixed $\boldsymbol\xi$ as $M\to\infty$, and the bounded integrand makes the double limit in $(n,M)$
interchangeable, so the conclusion is unchanged. Finally, $g$ is continuous, so by the continuous mapping
theorem$$
\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=g(\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{STC}})-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}})\xrightarrow{p} g(\bar\mu_{C(\mathcal P_{BC})})-g(\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal P_{BC})})=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}},
$$
which is @eq-stc-marg-consistency. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This is the theorem that licenses the whole method: integrate the fitted surface over the
*target* covariate distribution on the natural outcome scale, and you recover the marginal effect a trial in
that population would have reported, with no bias from non-collapsibility. It is the exact analogue, for
transport, of the g-computation result that standardization recovers the average treatment effect
(@thm-g-computation-unbiased); the only change is the population you standardize to. It is also the seed of
ML-NMR (Chapter 20), which puts this same natural-outcome-scale integration inside a single Bayesian network
model and dispenses with the separate Bucher step.

::: {.remark}
**On the machine-checked tag.** The Coq development `theories/STC.v` defines the marginal STC predicted means
`mu_A_STC`, `mu_C_STC` as the target-population means of the fitted surfaces and the estimator
`effect_AC_STC` as their difference, and `Theorem STC_consistent` proves the response-scale contrast
identity $\texttt{effect\_AC\_STC}=\mathbb E_2[Y_A^{\mathrm{target}}]-\mathbb E_2[Y_C^{\mathrm{target}}]$
given the two per-arm identification premises (the transported g-computation identities of @prp-stc-gcomp).
The Coq theorem is thus the identity-scale skeleton of @eq-stc-marg-consistency; the link transformation by
$g$ and the uniform-convergence step are the pen-and-paper additions made above. The companion development
treats the target-population expectation as an abstract linear operator, exactly as Chapter 14 treats
expectation in Bucher's theorem. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Non-collapsibility and its collapsible boundary {#sec-stc-noncollapsibility}

@thm-conditional-stc-bias located the plug-in bias in the curvature of $g^{-1}$. The same curvature is the
source of non-collapsibility (@def-non-collapsibility): the marginal effect is not the conditional effect
even when the conditional effect is constant across patients, that is, even with no effect modification. We
exhibit the gap in closed form for the odds ratio (catalogue G.4), then identify the boundary on which it
disappears.

Before the algebra, see the phenomenon in a table of two patients. Take the logistic model
$\operatorname{logit}\Pr(\text{event}\mid k,x)=\alpha_k+\beta x$ with $\alpha_C=-1$, $\alpha_A=0.5$,
$\beta=2$ (a steeper covariate slope than the running example, chosen to enlarge the gap), and a population
that is half low-risk ($x=0$) and half high-risk ($x=1$). The fitted event probabilities are
$\operatorname{expit}$ of the linear predictors:

| Patient stratum | $\Pr(\text{event}\mid C)$ | $\Pr(\text{event}\mid A)$ | within-stratum log odds ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| low-risk ($x=0$) | $\operatorname{expit}(-1)=0.2689$ | $\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=0.6225$ | $1.5$ |
| high-risk ($x=1$) | $\operatorname{expit}(1)=0.7311$ | $\operatorname{expit}(2.5)=0.9241$ | $1.5$ |
| population average (50/50) | $0.5000$ | $0.7733$ | $1.227$ (marginal) |

Read the last column. Within *each* stratum the log odds ratio of $A$ versus $C$ is exactly $1.5$: the effect
is constant across patients, so there is no effect modification. Yet the bottom row, formed by averaging the
probabilities down each arm and *then* taking the odds ratio, gives $1.227$, a different number. Averaging the
probabilities and taking the odds ratio does not recover the common within-stratum odds ratio. That mismatch is
**non-collapsibility**, and it is exactly why plug-in STC, which reports the constant conditional $1.5$,
overstates the marginal effect the population would show. The theorem below is this table written in symbols.

::: {#exm-stc-two-stratum}
## Two patients, one broken average
The table above is the whole idea in miniature. The plug-in reports the within-stratum effect $1.5$; the
population marginal effect is $1.227$; the gap $0.273$ is present with *no* effect modification, so it is a
property of the odds-ratio scale, not of patient heterogeneity. A risk difference would show no such gap: the
two within-stratum differences $0.6225-0.2689=0.3536$ and $0.9241-0.7311=0.1930$ average to
$(0.3536+0.1930)/2=0.2733$, which is exactly the marginal difference $0.7733-0.5000=0.2733$, because the
identity link commutes with averaging. The odds ratio does not. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-stc-noncollapsibility-counterexample}
## A closed-form non-collapsibility gap for the odds ratio
Let $g$ be the logit, so $g^{-1}=\operatorname{expit}$, and suppose the conditional model
$\operatorname{logit}\Pr(Y=1\mid k,X=x)=\alpha_k+\beta x$ holds with a single covariate $x$, equal slope
$\beta\ne0$ in both arms (so the conditional log odds ratio $\Lambda=\alpha_A-\alpha_C$ is constant in $x$,
no effect modification). Then the marginal log odds ratio
$$
d^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=\operatorname{logit}\bigl(\mathbb E_X[\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_A+\beta X)]\bigr)-\operatorname{logit}\bigl(\mathbb E_X[\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_C+\beta X)]\bigr)
$$
differs from the conditional log odds ratio $\Lambda=\alpha_A-\alpha_C$. Concretely, take
$\alpha_C=-1$, $\alpha_A=0.5$, $\beta=2$, and $X\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.5)$. Then the conditional log odds
ratio is $\Lambda=0.5-(-1)=1.5$, while
$$
\mathbb E_X[\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_C+\beta X)]=\tfrac12\operatorname{expit}(-1)+\tfrac12\operatorname{expit}(1)=\tfrac12(0.268941)+\tfrac12(0.731059)=0.5,
$$
$$
\mathbb E_X[\operatorname{expit}(\alpha_A+\beta X)]=\tfrac12\operatorname{expit}(0.5)+\tfrac12\operatorname{expit}(2.5)=\tfrac12(0.622459)+\tfrac12(0.924142)=0.773301,
$$
so the marginal log odds ratio is
$$
d^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=\operatorname{logit}(0.773301)-\operatorname{logit}(0.5)=\log\tfrac{0.773301}{0.226699}-0=\log(3.41113)=1.22704.
$$
The conditional effect $1.5$ exceeds the marginal effect $1.22704$ in magnitude: the gap is
$0.27296\ne0$, and conditional STC, which reports $\Lambda=1.5$, is biased upward for the marginal estimand.
(Corresponds to G.4 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
The arithmetic is the statement. We verify the four inverse-logit values and that the gap is genuine, not
rounding. With $e=2.718281828$: $\operatorname{expit}(-1)=1/(1+e)=0.2689414$;
$\operatorname{expit}(1)=e/(1+e)=0.7310586$, summing to $1$ so their half-sum is exactly $0.5$;
$\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=1/(1+e^{-0.5})=1/(1+0.6065307)=0.6224593$;
$\operatorname{expit}(2.5)=1/(1+e^{-2.5})=1/(1+0.0820850)=0.9241418$; the half-sum is $0.7733006$. Then
$\operatorname{logit}(0.7733006)=\log(0.7733006)-\log(0.2266994)=\log(3.411127)=1.227043$, while
$\operatorname{logit}(0.5)=0$. The difference $1.227043$ is not $1.5$; the discrepancy $0.272957$ is far
larger than the seventh-decimal precision of the inputs, so it is a genuine gap and not a numerical artifact.
That the conditional effect exceeds the marginal in magnitude is the generic direction of odds-ratio
non-collapsibility established in Chapter 11 (@thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr): marginalizing a logistic model
over a covariate with $\beta\ne0$ attenuates the effect toward the null. $\square$
:::

The counterexample uses no effect modification: the conditional log odds ratio is the constant $1.5$ in both
strata, yet the marginal effect is smaller. Non-collapsibility is therefore a phenomenon of the *scale*, not
of effect heterogeneity, and it is what forces STC to choose between the conditional and marginal estimands
even when @eq-stc-cate-link is constant. The boundary on which the choice becomes vacuous is the linear,
identity-link model, and there the choice provably does not matter. This is the machine-checked core of the
chapter.

::: {#prp-stc-linear-collapse}
## Collapsibility under a linear model
Suppose the outcome model is linear with the identity link,
$\mathbb E[Y\mid k,X=\mathbf x]=\alpha+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\mathbf 1\{k=A\}(\gamma+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2)$,
so $g=\mathrm{id}$ and $\mu_k(\mathbf x)=\eta_k(\mathbf x)$. Then for every population $\mathcal P$ the
marginal and conditional-at-the-mean effects coincide,
$$
d_{AC(\mathcal P)}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=d_{AC(\mathcal P)}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}=-\bigl(\gamma+\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2\bigr),
$$ {#eq-stc-linear-collapse}
and in the absence of effect modification ($\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0$) both equal the constant $-\gamma$,
independent of the covariate distribution. Marginal and conditional STC then return the same number, and the
plug-in is exact.

[machine-checked: `theories/STC.v`, `Lemma STC_collapse_linear`]
:::

::: {.proof}
With the identity link, the arm marginal mean @eq-stc-armmean is, by linearity of expectation,
$$
\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}=\mathbb E_{f_{\mathcal P}}[\eta_k(X)]=\alpha+\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+\mathbf 1\{k=A\}\bigl(\gamma+\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2\bigr)=\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P}),
$$
so $g(\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)})=\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}=\eta_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P})=g(\mu_k(\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P}))$,
the marginal and conditional-at-the-mean arm positions coincide, and so do their contrasts: @eq-stc-linear-collapse.
The contrast is $\eta_C(\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P})-\eta_A(\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P})=-(\gamma+\bar{\mathbf x}_{\mathcal P}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2)$,
which reduces to $-\gamma$ when $\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0$, a constant free of the covariate distribution.
Equivalently, this is @eq-stc-contrastbias with every $b_k=0$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the Coq proof isolates.** The companion `Lemma STC_collapse_linear` proves that for a linear outcome
model the marginal STC estimate equals the treatment coefficient $\gamma$, using *only* linearity of the
abstract target-population expectation operator and its constant rule. That single hypothesis, linearity of
expectation, is exactly what a nonlinear link destroys: $g^{-1}$ does not pass through an average, and the
proof of @prp-stc-linear-collapse breaks at its first line. The machine-checked lemma is therefore the
positive boundary of the non-collapsibility theorem @thm-stc-noncollapsibility-counterexample; the
counterexample itself, an arithmetic over the logit, is pen-and-paper. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A worked simulated treatment comparison {#sec-stc-example}

We carry a complete logistic STC from a fitted model to a reported relative effect, computing the biased
plug-in, the correct target marginal, and, for contrast, the unadjusted source marginal, so that every
number can be checked by hand. The covariate is the single binary risk marker of the running
example ($x=1$ high-risk, $x=0$ low-risk), the event is an unfavorable disease flare within six months, and a
larger log odds ratio means worse.

::: {#exm-stc-logistic}
## Conditional plug-in versus correct marginalization
The index trial of the running example (@sec-stc-picture) compares active $A$ against comparator $C$ with
individual data; fitting the logistic model
@def-stc-outcome-model returns the coefficients (treated here as exact for transparency)
$$
\hat\alpha=-1.0,\qquad \hat{\beta}_1=1.0,\qquad \hat\gamma=1.5,\qquad \hat{\beta}_2=0,
$$
so $\operatorname{logit}\mu_C(x)=-1.0+x$ and $\operatorname{logit}\mu_A(x)=0.5+x$, and the conditional log
odds ratio of $A$ versus $C$ is the constant $\Lambda=\hat\gamma=1.5$ (no effect modification, $\hat\beta_2=0$).
The fitted conditional event probabilities are
$$
\mu_C(0)=\operatorname{expit}(-1)=0.26894,\quad \mu_C(1)=\operatorname{expit}(0)=0.50000,
$$
$$
\mu_A(0)=\operatorname{expit}(0.5)=0.62246,\quad \mu_A(1)=\operatorname{expit}(1.5)=0.81757.
$$
The comparator (target) population has biomarker prevalence $\Pr_{BC}(X=1)=0.8$, hence
$\bar{x}_{BC}=0.8$; the index (source) population has $\Pr_{AC}(X=1)=0.5$.

**Step 1: conditional (plug-in) STC.** Evaluate the linear predictors at the target mean $\bar x_{BC}=0.8$:
$\eta_C(0.8)=-1.0+0.8=-0.2$ and $\eta_A(0.8)=0.5+0.8=1.3$. The plug-in log odds ratio of $A$ versus $C$ is
$$
\ell^{\,\mathrm{cond}}=\eta_A(0.8)-\eta_C(0.8)=1.3-(-0.2)=1.5,
$$
equal to $\hat\gamma$ as @prp-stc-linear-collapse predicts on the *link* scale: a difference of linear
predictors carries no curvature. In the reference-first convention $\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{cond}}=-1.5$.

**Step 2: marginal STC in the target population.** Average the fitted probabilities over $f_{BC}$ on the
response scale @eq-stc-marg-mean:
$$
\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{STC}}=0.2(0.26894)+0.8(0.50000)=0.45379,\quad
\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}}=0.2(0.62246)+0.8(0.81757)=0.77855.
$$
Apply the logit and contrast @eq-stc-marg:
$$
\ell^{\,\mathrm{marg}}_{BC}=\operatorname{logit}(0.77855)-\operatorname{logit}(0.45379)=1.25724-(-0.18538)=1.44262.
$$

**Step 3: the unadjusted source marginal.** The marginal effect the index trial itself reports averages over
$f_{AC}$ ($\Pr=0.5$):
$$
\hat\mu_C^{AC}=0.5(0.26894)+0.5(0.50000)=0.38447,\quad
\hat\mu_A^{AC}=0.5(0.62246)+0.5(0.81757)=0.72002,
$$
$$
\ell^{\,\mathrm{marg}}_{AC}=\operatorname{logit}(0.72002)-\operatorname{logit}(0.38447)=0.94455-(-0.47061)=1.41516.
$$

**Step 4: comparison.** Collecting the three log odds ratios of $A$ versus $C$ and exponentiating,
$$
\underbrace{\ell^{\,\mathrm{cond}}=1.50000}_{\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}=4.4817},\qquad
\underbrace{\ell^{\,\mathrm{marg}}_{BC}=1.44262}_{\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}=4.2318},\qquad
\underbrace{\ell^{\,\mathrm{marg}}_{AC}=1.41516}_{\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}=4.1171}.
$$
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Three lessons sit in these numbers.

::: {.remark}
**The plug-in bias.** The conditional STC estimate $1.50000$ overstates the target marginal effect
$1.44262$ by $0.05738$ on the log odds-ratio scale, an odds ratio inflated from $4.232$ to $4.482$. This is
the non-collapsibility gap @eq-stc-contrastbias of @thm-conditional-stc-bias, present here even though there
is no effect modification ($\hat\beta_2=0$): the odds ratio simply is not collapsible. By @exm-stc-loglink,
had the link been the log rather than the logit, the contrast bias with $\hat\beta_2=0$ would have been
exactly zero, the arm-level Jensen gaps cancelling. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What population adjustment moves.** The correct marginal effect is not a single number; it is
population-specific. In the source population it is $1.41516$; in the target it is $1.44262$. STC's job is to
report the *target* value $1.44262$, and it does so by integrating the fitted surface over $f_{BC}$ in Step 2
rather than over $f_{AC}$ in Step 3. The shift $1.41516\to1.44262$ is the entire population adjustment: it is
small here because the biomarker is not an effect modifier ($\hat\beta_2=0$), so only the non-collapsibility
interaction with the changed covariate mix moves the marginal effect. With $\hat\beta_2\ne0$ the shift would
be first-order in the covariate-mean difference and typically far larger; @exr-stc-em-shift works such a
case. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Closing the triangle.** To reach the clinical target $A$ versus $B$, the STC output
$\hat d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=-1.44262$ (reference-first) is differenced against the
comparator trial's published $\hat d_{BC}$ by Bucher's identity (@thm-bucher-unbiased),
$\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\hat d_{BC}$, both now evaluated in the common population
$\mathcal P_{BC}$. The marginalization of Step 2 is exactly what makes the two contrasts live in the same
population, repairing the transitivity failure (@def-transitivity) that the raw source effect $1.41516$ of
Step 3 would have carried into the subtraction. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Bayesian g-computation {#sec-stc-bayes}

We now handle *uncertainty* properly, then (in @sec-stc-consistency) fold STC back into the Chapter 17
framework. In applied terms, Bayesian g-computation runs the five-step workflow once per posterior draw of the
model coefficients: each draw is one plausible fitted surface, hence one plausible target effect, and the
spread of those target effects across draws *is* the uncertainty interval. Because the marginal STC functional
is nonlinear in $\boldsymbol\xi$, its uncertainty is generally skewed; simulating from the posterior captures
that skew automatically, whereas the delta method (@exr-stc-delta) forces a symmetric Gaussian on the link
scale.

Marginal STC is a smooth functional of the fitted parameter, so its uncertainty can be propagated either by
the delta method (@exr-stc-delta) or, more naturally for the nonlinear integration step, by simulation from a
posterior. The Bayesian implementation is **g-computation from the posterior** and is catalogue result G.5.

::: {#def-stc-bayes}
## Bayesian g-computation for STC
Place a prior $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi)$ on the outcome-model parameters and obtain the posterior
$\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathcal D)$ from the index IPD $\mathcal D$. Define the **STC functional**
$$
\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi)\;=\;g\!\Bigl(\textstyle\int\mu_C(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\Bigr)-g\!\Bigl(\textstyle\int\mu_A(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-stc-functional}
which maps a parameter to the marginal STC relative effect @eq-stc-marg it induces. The **posterior of the
target effect** is the pushforward $\Psi_\#\,\pi(\cdot\mid\mathcal D)$ (the "pushforward" is simply the
distribution of $\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi)$ when $\boldsymbol\xi$ is drawn from the posterior: feed posterior draws
through $\Psi$ and collect the outputs), approximated by drawing
$\boldsymbol\xi^{(1)},\dots,\boldsymbol\xi^{(S)}\sim\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathcal D)$ and forming
$\{\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\}_{s=1}^S$, with each integral in @eq-stc-functional itself a Monte Carlo
average @eq-stc-mc over $f_{BC}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-bayesian-g-computation}
## Validity of Bayesian g-computation
Let $\Psi$ be the STC functional @eq-stc-functional with $g$ and $g^{-1}$ continuous. Then:

1. **Pushforward.** $\Psi$ is a measurable (indeed continuous) function of $\boldsymbol\xi$, so the posterior
   distribution of the target effect is well defined as $\Psi_\#\,\pi(\cdot\mid\mathcal D)$, and the empirical
   measure of $\{\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})\}_{s=1}^S$ converges weakly to it as $S\to\infty$, with the
   posterior mean and any posterior quantile of $\Psi$ estimated at the Monte Carlo rate $O_p(S^{-1/2})$.

2. **Frequentist calibration.** Under the regularity conditions of @thm-stc-outcome-mle and a prior with a
   continuous positive density at $\boldsymbol\xi_0$, the Bernstein-von Mises theorem (@vandervaart1998,
   Chapter 10) gives $\|\pi(\cdot\mid\mathcal D)-\mathcal N(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi},n^{-1}\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^{-1})\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\xrightarrow{p}0$.
   Consequently, by the delta method (@thm-delta-method) applied to the smooth $\Psi$, the posterior of the
   target effect is asymptotically $\mathcal N\bigl(\Psi(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}),\,n^{-1}\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^\top\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^{-1}\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)\bigr)$,
   the same Gaussian law as the sampling distribution of the frequentist marginal STC point estimate
   @eq-stc-marg. Equal-tailed posterior credible intervals therefore have asymptotically correct frequentist
   coverage. (Corresponds to G.5 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* For each fixed $\boldsymbol\xi$ the integrand $\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)=g^{-1}(\eta_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi))$
is continuous in $\boldsymbol\xi$ (composition of continuous $g^{-1}$ with the affine $\eta_k$) and bounded
on the covariate range, so by dominated convergence the integrals $\int\mu_k(\mathbf x;\boldsymbol\xi)f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x$
are continuous in $\boldsymbol\xi$; composing with the continuous $g$ and differencing,
$\Psi$ is continuous, hence Borel measurable. A measurable function of a random variable has a well-defined
law, the pushforward $\Psi_\#\,\pi(\cdot\mid\mathcal D)$. The draws $\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)}$ are distributed
(exactly, or in the stationary limit of the Markov chain, by @def-stc-bayes) according to
$\pi(\cdot\mid\mathcal D)$, so $\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})$ are distributed according to the pushforward; the
Glivenko-Cantelli theorem gives weak convergence of their empirical measure as $S\to\infty$, and the central
limit theorem gives the $O_p(S^{-1/2})$ Monte Carlo rate for the posterior mean and, via the smoothness of
the quantile map of the continuous pushforward, for posterior quantiles. The inner Monte Carlo over $f_{BC}$
adds an independent $O_p(M^{-1/2})$ error to each $\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})$, controlled by taking $M$
large.

*Part 2.* The Bernstein-von Mises theorem applies because @thm-stc-outcome-mle verified the local asymptotic
normality conditions (smooth log-likelihood, nonsingular Fisher information $\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)$,
consistent MLE) and the prior charges a neighborhood of $\boldsymbol\xi_0$ with a continuous positive density;
its conclusion is the stated total-variation convergence of the posterior to the Gaussian centered at the MLE
with covariance $n^{-1}\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^{-1}$. The functional $\Psi$ is differentiable at
$\boldsymbol\xi_0$ with gradient $\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)$ obtained by differentiating @eq-stc-functional
under the integral sign (legitimate by bounded, continuous integrands), so the delta method transports the
Gaussian limit through $\Psi$: the posterior of $\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi)$ converges to
$\mathcal N(\Psi(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}),n^{-1}\nabla\Psi^\top\mathcal I^{-1}\nabla\Psi)$. The frequentist
marginal STC estimate $\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=\Psi(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})$ has, again by the delta
method applied to the sampling law @eq-stc-mle-an of $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$, the identical asymptotic Gaussian
distribution. Two asymptotically equal Gaussian laws produce intervals with the same coverage, so the
credible interval is asymptotically a confidence interval. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** Part 2 says the honest Bayesian interval and the frequentist confidence interval agree
asymptotically, so a health technology assessment that runs STC in a Bayesian pipeline is not buying a
different answer, only a more convenient and more faithful propagation of the nonlinearity. It is the same
guarantee that lets network meta-analysis (Chapters 15 and 20) report Bayesian credible intervals to
decision-makers who reason in frequentist terms.

::: {.remark}
**Why simulate rather than delta.** The delta-method standard error requires the gradient
$\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)$, whose entries are themselves integrals of $g^{-1}{}'$ against $f_{BC}$ and
must be approximated; the approximation is awkward and the resulting interval is symmetric on the link scale
by construction. Bayesian g-computation instead propagates the full nonlinear functional through the
posterior sample, so it captures asymmetry and higher-order curvature exactly within Monte Carlo error, and
it composes cleanly with a Bayesian comparator summary: a posterior draw of $\hat d_{BC}$ differenced against
a posterior draw $\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^{(s)})$ yields, by Bucher's identity, a posterior draw of the anchored
$\hat d_{AB}$, propagating all uncertainty coherently. This is the implementation used by the multilevel
methods of Chapters 20 and 26. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**A practical uncertainty checklist.** A defensible interval for the final $A$-versus-$B$ effect must combine
four distinct sources of uncertainty, which Bayesian g-computation can propagate jointly:

1. **Outcome-model parameters.** Uncertainty in $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$ from the finite index sample; this is
   the posterior $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathcal D)$, or the sandwich variance (@def-sandwich-variance) when
   misspecification is suspected.
2. **Monte Carlo integration.** The $O_p(M^{-1/2})$ error from approximating the integral @eq-stc-marg-mean by
   an average over $M$ synthetic patients; drive it down by taking $M$ large.
3. **Reconstructed covariate distribution.** Uncertainty in $f_{BC}$ itself when it was rebuilt from published
   summaries (the warning after @def-stc-marginal); the reported means and correlations are themselves
   estimates, and the assumed copula is a modeling choice.
4. **Published comparator effect.** The standard error of $\hat d_{BC}$ from the comparator trial, which enters
   at the Bucher step.

A common failure is to report only source 1 (the model fit) and to treat $f_{BC}$ and $\hat d_{BC}$ as fixed,
understating the interval. Sources 1, 2, and 4 compose cleanly by differencing posterior draws (the "Why
simulate" remark above); source 3 requires either a Bayesian model for the covariate summaries or a sensitivity
analysis over plausible reconstructions. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## STC consistency under the population-adjustment conditions {#sec-stc-consistency}

@thm-marginal-stc-unbiased established consistency for the marginal effect *in the comparator population*
