under correct specification and transportability of the outcome surface. The population-adjustment theory of
Chapter 17 expresses transportability through the conditions on effect modifiers and prognostic variables
that an indirect comparison actually needs, separately for the anchored and unanchored cases. We restate STC
consistency in those terms (catalogue G.6), so that STC slots into the general framework alongside MAIC.

::: {.remark}
**Two data scenarios, in the running example.** *Anchored* is the situation we have carried throughout: the
index trial randomizes $A$ against $C$ and the comparator trial randomizes $B$ against the *same* $C$, so $C$ is
a shared anchor and Bucher's subtraction cancels the study baselines. Here STC need only get the
$A$-versus-$C$ *contrast* right in $\mathcal P_{BC}$, so it must include every covariate that *modifies* that
contrast (every effect modifier). *Unanchored* is the harder situation where the two trials share no common arm,
for instance a single-arm study of $A$ and a single-arm study of $B$. Now there is no baseline to cancel, so
STC must get each *absolute* arm outcome right in $\mathcal P_{BC}$, which means including every covariate that
is merely *prognostic* (that shifts the outcome level) in addition to every effect modifier. Concretely: if age
is prognostic for the flare but does not change the $A$-versus-$C$ effect, the anchored analysis may safely omit
it, but the unanchored analysis may not, because age now moves arm levels that no longer cancel.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#thm-stc-consistency}
## Anchored and unanchored STC consistency
Assume the outcome model @def-stc-outcome-model is correctly specified on the chosen link scale, so
$\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\xi_0$ by @thm-stc-outcome-mle, and the integrals are computed
as in @thm-marginal-stc-unbiased.

1. **Anchored.** Suppose every effect modifier of the $A$-versus-$C$ contrast that is distributed
   differently between the index and comparator populations is included in $\mathbf x$ (the anchored
   sufficiency condition of @thm-anchored-paic-consistency), and that the fitted surfaces describe
   $\mathcal P_{BC}$: on the identity link, conditional constancy of relative effects
   (@def-conditional-constancy-relative) suffices; on any other link, the arm surfaces $\mu_A,\mu_C$
   themselves must transport (@prp-stc-gcomp). Then the marginal STC estimator @eq-stc-marg is consistent
   for $d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}$, and the anchored Bucher combination
   $\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}-\hat d_{BC}$ is consistent for $d_{AB(\mathcal P_{BC})}$.

2. **Unanchored.** Let the index source contain arm $A$ only and the aggregate source report the $B$ arm in
   its population $\mathcal P_B$. If conditional constancy of absolute effects holds for $A$
   (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute) and every prognostic variable and effect modifier distributed
   differently between the populations is included in $\mathbf x$ (the unanchored condition of
   @thm-unanchored-paic-consistency), then the unanchored marginal STC estimator
   $g(\hat\mu_B)-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}})$, with $\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}}$ integrated over $f_B$ and
   $\hat\mu_B$ the reported arm mean, is consistent for $d_{AB(\mathcal P_B)}$.

(Corresponds to G.6 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
The argument is the regression-route counterpart of the MAIC consistency theorems
@thm-anchored-maic-consistency and @thm-unanchored-maic-consistency, with the weighted mean replaced by the
predicted marginal mean @eq-stc-marg-mean.

*Anchored.* By the uniform-convergence argument of @thm-marginal-stc-unbiased,
$\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}\xrightarrow{p}m_k:=\int\mu_k(\mathbf x)f_{BC}(\mathbf x)\,d\mathbf x$, the index
trial's surface averaged over the comparator covariates, so
$\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\xrightarrow{p}g(m_C)-g(m_A)$. On the identity link this is
$\int(\mu_C-\mu_A)f_{BC}$, the average of the conditional contrast, which conditional constancy of relative
effects (with every differentially distributed effect modifier in $\mathbf x$) makes equal to
$d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}$, the study baseline cancelling from each contrast. On any other
link the baseline does not cancel, and the surfaces themselves must transport; then
$m_k=\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}$ by @prp-stc-gcomp and again
$\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\xrightarrow{p}d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}$. The comparator trial's
$\hat d_{BC}$ already estimates $d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}$ in its own population, so both contrasts now live in
$\mathcal P_{BC}$, transitivity holds across them by construction, and @thm-bucher-unbiased gives consistency
of the difference for $d_{AB(\mathcal P_{BC})}$.

*Unanchored.* Without a common anchor the estimand is a contrast of *absolute* arm positions across
populations, so the cancellation of study baselines that the anchor provides (the
$\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}$ cancellation of Chapter 14) is unavailable, and the prognostic structure no longer drops
out. Conditional constancy of *absolute* effects (@def-conditional-constancy-absolute) is then required, and
*every* differentially distributed prognostic variable as well as every effect modifier must be in
$\mathbf x$ (@thm-unanchored-paic-consistency), so that the fitted surface $\mu_A(\cdot)$ itself, not merely
a contrast, is transportable. Then @prp-stc-gcomp and @thm-marginal-stc-unbiased (with $f_B$ in place of
$f_{BC}$) give $\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}}\xrightarrow{p}\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal P_B)}$, the reported
$\hat\mu_B$ is consistent for $\bar\mu_{B(\mathcal P_B)}$ by design, and the continuous mapping theorem
delivers consistency of $g(\hat\mu_B)-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}})$ for $d_{AB(\mathcal P_B)}$. $\square$
:::

**Why this matters.** This is where STC stops being a stand-alone trick and becomes a citizen of the
population-adjustment framework of Chapter 17: its consistency rests on exactly the same effect-modifier and
prognostic-variable conditions that govern MAIC and ML-NMR, only discharged through a fitted regression instead
of weights. The practical reading is a covariate-selection rule: for an anchored comparison, model every effect
modifier that differs between the trials; for an unanchored one, model every prognostic variable too. Getting
that list wrong is misspecification, and by the remark after @thm-stc-outcome-mle its price is bias, not merely
variance.

::: {.remark}
**STC against MAIC, assumption for assumption.** STC and MAIC are dual routes through the same
conditional-transportability framework, and Chapter 17 shows they target the same estimand when both are
valid. Their hypotheses differ in two mirror-image ways. STC is *stronger* in demanding a correctly specified
parametric outcome model, link and functional form and included covariates; if the model is wrong, STC
inherits the pseudo-true bias of the misspecification remark after @thm-stc-outcome-mle, whereas MAIC needs
no outcome model but relies on a correct weight model or on arm means linear in the matched moments
(@thm-anchored-maic-consistency). STC is *weaker* in demanding no overlap: a regression extrapolates where
weights cannot exist (@thm-maic-no-extrapolation, @prp-stc-gcomp), so STC's variance is not inflated through
a small effective sample size the way MAIC's is (@thm-maic-ess-bound), although its predictions become
imprecise, and model-dependent, far from the index data. The companion development records this trade-off as a comparison of method
profiles in `theories/Comparison.v`; the two methods provably agree when both sets of assumptions hold, which
we make precise next. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Equivalence of MAIC and STC under a linear model {#sec-stc-maic-equivalence}

When the outcome model is linear and only first moments are matched, the weighting route and the regression
route are not merely both valid; they are asymptotically the same estimator. This is catalogue result G.7. It
explains the close agreement of MAIC and STC seen in practice when the outcome surface is near-linear and
overlap is good, and it locates exactly where the two methods part company.

We first record the trivial but useful fact that the two methods agree whenever both are valid, the
abstract statement that has a machine-checked counterpart.

::: {#cor-maic-stc-agree}
## Agreement under joint validity
Suppose the anchored MAIC assumptions and the anchored STC assumptions both hold, so that, by
@thm-anchored-maic-consistency and @thm-stc-consistency respectively, each estimator is consistent for the
same target estimand $d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}$. Then the two estimators have the same
probability limit, $\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\xrightarrow{p}0$.

[machine-checked: `theories/Comparison.v`, `Theorem methods_agree_when_correct`]
:::

::: {.proof}
By hypothesis each estimator converges in probability to the common target $d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}$,
so their difference converges in probability to $0$ by the algebra of limits. The Coq theorem
`methods_agree_when_correct` is this statement stripped to its logical core: from the two identification
premises (MAIC's assumptions imply its estimate equals the true effect, STC's assumptions imply the same for
its estimate) it derives equality of the two estimates. $\square$
:::

The substantive theorem is sharper: under a linear model the agreement is exact in the limit even before
invoking a shared target, because the two estimators are two consistent estimators of the *same linear
functional* of the same parameters.

::: {#thm-maic-stc-equivalence}
## Asymptotic equivalence of MAIC and STC under a linear model
Suppose (i) the outcome model is linear with the identity link,
$\mathbb E[Y\mid k,X=\mathbf x]=\alpha_k+\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}$ for $k\in\{A,C\}$; (ii) the MAIC
weights are the entropy-balanced exponential weights of @thm-maic-exponential-weights, with parameters chosen
to satisfy the first-moment balance constraint (@def-moment-balance, @def-entropy-balancing); and (iii) only
the first moments of the covariates are matched, the weighted index mean equalling $\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$.
Then the marginal STC estimator @eq-stc-marg and the MAIC weighted-difference estimator have the same
probability limit,
$$
\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\ \xrightarrow{p}\ (\alpha_C-\alpha_A)+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_{(C)}-\boldsymbol\beta_{(A)})\ \xleftarrow{p}\ \hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{MAIC}},
$$ {#eq-stc-maic-equiv}
and are therefore asymptotically equivalent. (Corresponds to G.7 in the proof catalogue.)
:::

::: {.proof}
*The common target.* With the identity link, @prp-stc-linear-collapse gives the marginal arm position
$\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\alpha_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}$, so the marginal
relative effect @eq-stc-marg-estimand in the comparator population is
$$
d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=\bar\mu_{C(\mathcal P_{BC})}-\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\alpha_C-\alpha_A)+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top(\boldsymbol\beta_{(C)}-\boldsymbol\beta_{(A)}),
$$
the right-hand quantity in @eq-stc-maic-equiv.

*STC side.* Under the linear model the predicted marginal means @eq-stc-marg-mean are, by linearity of
expectation, $\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{STC}}=\hat\alpha_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(k)}$, so
$\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}=(\hat\alpha_C-\hat\alpha_A)+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(C)}-\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(A)})$.
By @thm-stc-outcome-mle the coefficient estimates are consistent, $(\hat\alpha_k,\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{(k)})\xrightarrow{p}(\alpha_k,\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)})$,
so $\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}\xrightarrow{p}d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}$, the left
convergence in @eq-stc-maic-equiv.

*MAIC side.* The MAIC estimator is the difference of weighted arm means
$\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\sum_{i:T_i=k}w_i Y_i\big/\sum_{i:T_i=k}w_i$, with the entropy-balanced weights
$w_i=\exp(\hat\alpha_w+\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_w^\top(\mathbf x_i-\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}))$ of
@thm-maic-exponential-weights. Let $P^\ast_k$ denote the limiting weighted law of the covariates in arm $k$;
under overlap and the law of large numbers for weighted averages,
$\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\xrightarrow{p}\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[Y\mid T=k]=\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}\bigl[\mathbb E[Y\mid k,X]\bigr]=\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[\alpha_k+X^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}]=\alpha_k+\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[X]^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}$,
the middle step by the tower property and the linear model, the last by linearity of expectation. The
first-moment balance constraint (iii) forces $\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[X]=\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}$, so
$\hat\mu_k^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\xrightarrow{p}\alpha_k+\bar{\mathbf x}_{BC}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{(k)}=\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P_{BC})}$,
the same arm limit as the STC side. Differencing the arms,
$\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{MAIC}}=\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}\xrightarrow{p}d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}$,
the right convergence in @eq-stc-maic-equiv.

Both estimators converge in probability to the same number, hence their difference converges to zero: they
are asymptotically equivalent. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**A one-line numeric check.** Take the linear model of @exr-stc-maic-numeric: $\mathbb E[Y\mid C,x]=1+0.5x$ and
$\mathbb E[Y\mid A,x]=2+0.5x$, with target covariate mean $\bar x_{BC}=1$. *STC side*: the predicted target
means are $\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{STC}}=1+0.5(1)=1.5$ and $\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{STC}}=2+0.5(1)=2.5$, so the effect is
$1.5-2.5=-1$. *MAIC side*: entropy-balanced weights that pull the index covariate mean to $\bar x_{BC}=1$ give
weighted arm means $\alpha_k+\beta_{(k)}\cdot 1$, again $1.5$ and $2.5$, so the effect is again $-1$. The two
routes land on the identical number because, under a linear model, the weighted mean of $Y$ depends on the
covariates *only through their first moment*, which is exactly what MAIC matches and what STC's linear
prediction uses. This is why the two methods so often agree in practice: near-linear outcome and good overlap
make them two computations of the same first-moment functional. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Where the equivalence breaks.** The proof used linearity twice and first-moment balance once, and the
equivalence fails as soon as any of the three is removed.

1. *Nonlinear link.* If $g$ is not the identity, $\mu_k(\mathbf x)=g^{-1}(\eta_k(\mathbf x))$ is curved,
   STC's response-scale integration carries the Jensen terms of @thm-conditional-stc-bias, and MAIC's
   first-moment balance no longer reproduces them; the two estimators target the same marginal effect but by
   different finite-sample routes and need not coincide except in the limit, and only then if both remain
   consistent.

2. *Higher moments needed.* If the conditional mean involves $\mathbf x$ nonlinearly, for instance a
   quadratic term $\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\gamma\mathbf x$, then $\mathbb E_{P^\ast_k}[\mathbb E[Y\mid k,X]]$
   depends on the second moment of $P^\ast_k$, which first-moment balance does not pin to $\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}$;
   MAIC then estimates a different number from STC unless the higher moments are also matched.

3. *Nonlinear interactions.* Even with the identity link, an interaction structure richer than the additive
   $\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_2$ makes the conditional contrast a nonlinear function of $\mathbf x$, and
   first-moment balance is again insufficient.

In practice the two methods agree closely when overlap is good and the outcome surface is near-linear, and
diverge under poor overlap, where MAIC's variance inflates (@thm-maic-ess-bound) while STC extrapolates, or
under misspecification of the outcome model, where STC is biased while MAIC remains consistent if its
log-linear weight model is correct (@zhao2017entropy). The choice between them is the choice between trusting a model and trusting an overlap.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-stc-notes}

Simulated treatment comparison was introduced by @caro2010stc under the title "No head-to-head trial?
Simulate the missing arms," as a regression-and-simulation alternative to matching; the original proposal is
the conditional plug-in of @def-stc-conditional, evaluated at the comparator covariate means. The
distinction between conditional and marginal STC, the diagnosis of the plug-in bias as non-collapsibility,
and the recommendation to integrate on the response scale are due to the population-adjustment methods
literature, principally the NICE technical support document @phillippo2016tsd18 and the thesis of
@phillippo2019thesis (Sections 2.2 to 2.4), which also frame STC and MAIC as the outcome-regression and
weighting implementations of one conditional-transportability problem; the estimand-based reframing in terms
of marginal versus conditional targets and the transportability of the outcome surface is developed by
@chandler2026transport. The identification of marginal STC as g-computation standardized to a target
population (@prp-stc-gcomp) places it in the lineage of @hernan2020whatif and @rosenbaum1983, and is the seed
of the multilevel network meta-regression of @phillippo2020mlnmr (Chapter 20), which embeds the same
response-scale integration inside a coherent Bayesian network model and removes STC's reliance on a separate
Bucher step. The comparison of MAIC and STC against the MLE asymptotics of @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality
follows the GLM treatment of @mccullagh1989glm and the M-estimation theory of @vandervaart1998, the latter
also supplying the Bernstein-von Mises theorem behind @thm-bayesian-g-computation.

This chapter corresponds to results G.1 through G.7 of the proof catalogue in `proofs/G_stc.md`: the outcome
MLE asymptotics G.1 (@thm-stc-outcome-mle), the conditional plug-in bias G.2 (@thm-conditional-stc-bias),
the marginal STC consistency G.3 (@thm-marginal-stc-unbiased), the non-collapsibility counterexample G.4
(@thm-stc-noncollapsibility-counterexample), Bayesian g-computation G.5 (@thm-bayesian-g-computation), STC
consistency under the Chapter 17 conditions G.6 (@thm-stc-consistency), and the MAIC-STC equivalence G.7
(@thm-maic-stc-equivalence).

Two results carry machine-checked tags confirmed in the companion Coq development. The marginal STC contrast
identity @thm-marginal-stc-unbiased is `Theorem STC_consistent` in `theories/STC.v`, which proves the
response-scale identity $\texttt{effect\_AC\_STC}=\mathbb E_2[Y_A^{\mathrm{target}}]-\mathbb E_2[Y_C^{\mathrm{target}}]$
from the per-arm transported g-computation premises; the link transformation and uniform convergence are the
analytic additions made here. The collapsibility boundary @prp-stc-linear-collapse is
`Lemma STC_collapse_linear` in the same file, which proves that a linear outcome model makes the marginal STC
estimate equal the treatment coefficient using only linearity of the abstract target expectation, the single
property a nonlinear link destroys. The agreement-under-joint-validity corollary @cor-maic-stc-agree is
`Theorem methods_agree_when_correct` in `theories/Comparison.v`, the logical core of the equivalence. The
non-collapsibility counterexample @thm-stc-noncollapsibility-counterexample is deliberately left as
pen-and-paper arithmetic over the logit, as its content is a numerical witness rather than an algebraic
identity; the companion file confirms only the collapsible boundary. As in Chapter 14, the Coq files treat
the target-population expectation as an abstract linear operator, so the formalization captures the algebraic
content while leaving the measure-theoretic construction of the integral @eq-stc-marg-mean to the caller. The
files `theories/OutcomeRegression.v` (g-computation, the source-population analogue) and `theories/Comparison.v`
(the MAIC-versus-STC method profiles) provide the surrounding structure.

## Exercises {#sec-stc-exercises}

An exercise marked with a star ($\star$) has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first two are warm-ups;
do them before the proof-heavy exercises that follow.

::: {#exr-stc-warmup-table}
**(Warm-up, computation) A full STC table by hand.** An index trial fits the logistic model
$\operatorname{logit}\mu_C(x)=-0.5+0.7x$ and $\operatorname{logit}\mu_A(x)=0.4+0.7x$ for a single binary
covariate $x$ (so there is no effect modification). The target comparator population has $\Pr_{BC}(x=1)=0.6$.
(a) Compute the four fitted event probabilities $\mu_C(0),\mu_C(1),\mu_A(0),\mu_A(1)$ with $\operatorname{expit}$.
(b) Conditional plug-in: evaluate the linear predictors at $\bar x_{BC}=0.6$ and report the plug-in log odds
ratio of $A$ versus $C$. (c) Marginal STC: average the fitted probabilities over the target on the natural
outcome scale, apply the logit, and report the marginal log odds ratio. (d) State which of (b) and (c) a
health technology assessment should use, and by how much they differ. This is the five-step workflow of
@sec-stc-picture with the Bucher step omitted.
:::

::: {#exr-stc-warmup-interpret}
**(Warm-up, interpretation) Which scale, which average?** In one or two sentences each, explain to a colleague:
(a) why "average then link" and "link then average" give different answers for an odds ratio but the same
answer for a risk difference; (b) what "simulated" refers to in *simulated treatment comparison*; and (c) why
STC can predict into a comparator population that MAIC cannot weight into, and what STC must assume to justify
that prediction. No arithmetic required.
:::

::: {#exr-stc-recompute}
**Recompute with a new target.** In the worked example @exm-stc-logistic, keep the fitted model
($\hat\alpha=-1$, $\hat\beta_1=1$, $\hat\gamma=1.5$, $\hat\beta_2=0$) but change the target biomarker
prevalence to $\Pr_{BC}(X=1)=0.3$. Compute the conditional plug-in log odds ratio, the marginal STC log odds
ratio in the new target, and the non-collapsibility gap between them. Confirm that the plug-in is unchanged
at $1.5$ while the marginal value moves, and explain why the plug-in ignores the covariate distribution
entirely.
:::

::: {#exr-stc-em-shift}
**With effect modification.** Repeat @exm-stc-logistic but with $\hat\beta_2=0.8$ (the biomarker now modifies
the $A$-versus-$C$ effect), so $\operatorname{logit}\mu_A(x)=0.5+1.8x$. With target prevalence
$\bar x_{BC}=0.8$ and source prevalence $0.5$, compute the conditional plug-in, the target marginal STC, and
the source marginal log odds ratios. Show that the source-to-target shift is now much larger than in the
$\hat\beta_2=0$ case, and identify how much of the conditional-versus-marginal gap is non-collapsibility and
how much is effect modification interacting with the covariate shift.
:::

::: {#exr-stc-identity-exact}
**Identity link is exact.** Prove directly from @def-stc-estimands that for the identity link the conditional
plug-in STC estimator @eq-stc-cond and the marginal STC estimator @eq-stc-marg have the same probability
limit for every covariate distribution, recovering @prp-stc-linear-collapse without the Taylor expansion.
Then exhibit a continuous outcome with a log link for which they differ, and compute the gap using
@exm-stc-loglink.
:::

::: {#exr-stc-gcomp-positivity}
**No overlap required.** Let the index trial observe the covariate only on $[0,1]$ but the target place mass
on $[1,2]$. Explain why the marginal STC integral @eq-stc-marg-mean is still defined while the MAIC weights
are not, and state precisely the assumption (correctness of $\mu_k$ off the index support) that STC must add
to justify the extrapolation. Relate this to @prp-stc-gcomp and @thm-maic-no-extrapolation.
:::

::: {#exr-stc-noncollapsibility-sign}
**Direction of the gap.** For the logit link with equal arm slopes ($\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0$) and a
covariate symmetric about its mean, use @eq-stc-taylor and the sign of $(\operatorname{expit})''$, which is
positive for $\eta<0$ and negative for $\eta>0$, to argue that the conditional-at-the-mean odds ratio is
generically farther from the null than the marginal odds ratio. Confirm the direction against the
counterexample @thm-stc-noncollapsibility-counterexample, where the conditional $1.5$ exceeds the marginal
$1.227$.
:::

::: {#exr-stc-loglink-cancellation}
**($\star$) The collapsible contrast.** Using @exm-stc-loglink, prove that under the log link with Gaussian
covariates the conditional plug-in STC is unbiased for the marginal effect *if and only if*
$\boldsymbol\beta_1^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2+\tfrac12\boldsymbol\beta_2^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_{BC}\boldsymbol\beta_2=0$,
and in particular whenever there is no effect modification ($\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0$). Contrast this
with the logit link, where @thm-stc-noncollapsibility-counterexample shows the plug-in is biased even with
$\boldsymbol\beta_2=\mathbf 0$. Conclude that collapsibility of the contrast is a property of the link, and
relate your finding to the collapsibility of the rate ratio in Chapter 11. (A solution appears in
Appendix F.)
:::

::: {#exr-stc-delta}
**($\star$) Delta-method variance of marginal STC.** Let $\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi)$ be the STC functional
@eq-stc-functional. Using @thm-stc-outcome-mle and the delta method (@thm-delta-method), show that
$\sqrt n(\hat d_{AC}^{\,\mathrm{marg}}-d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}^{\,\mathrm{marg}})\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^\top\mathcal I(\boldsymbol\xi_0)^{-1}\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0))$,
and write the gradient $\nabla\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi_0)$ as an integral of $g^{-1}{}'$ against $f_{BC}$ for each
coordinate of $\boldsymbol\xi$. Explain why @thm-bayesian-g-computation reproduces this variance
asymptotically, and why the Bayesian route avoids computing the gradient. Under misspecification, replace
$\mathcal I^{-1}$ by the sandwich of @def-sandwich-variance and state what $\Psi(\boldsymbol\xi^\ast)$ then
estimates. (A solution appears in Appendix F.)
:::

::: {#exr-stc-maic-numeric}
**MAIC equals STC, numerically.** Construct a linear-model dataset with one covariate: arm means
$\mathbb E[Y\mid C,x]=1+0.5x$ and $\mathbb E[Y\mid A,x]=2+0.5x$ (so $\boldsymbol\beta_2=0$), source covariate
mean $0$, target covariate mean $\bar x_{BC}=1$. Compute the marginal STC effect from @thm-maic-stc-equivalence,
then verify that entropy-balanced MAIC weights matching the first moment give the same limit. Now add a
quadratic term $0.3x^2$ to the comparator arm only and show that first-moment MAIC and STC now disagree,
matching the breakdown clause of the equivalence remark.
:::
